subject: biology
title: Diffusion
key_idea: **Diffusion** is the spreading out of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration. It is how oxygen, carbon dioxide and many other substances move across cell membranes. The rate depends on the concentration gradient, temperature, surface area and distance.

blocks.text: Particles of a gas or of a substance in solution spread out. This section covers what moves and in which direction.

items.meaning: The spreading out of particles, giving a net movement from a higher concentration to a lower concentration.
The difference in concentration between two places.

items: Particles move **down** a concentration gradient, from high concentration to low concentration.
Diffusion carries on until the concentrations are equal.
It does not need energy from respiration.
Particles can diffuse across cell membranes.

rows: Into cells from the blood, for respiration. In gas exchange, from the air into the blood
Out of cells into the blood. In gas exchange, from the blood into the air
Out of cells into the blood plasma, for excretion in the kidney
Glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, glycerol, mineral ions

items: Diffusion is the net movement of particles down a concentration gradient.
Oxygen and carbon dioxide move into and out of cells by diffusion.
A substance only diffuses if there is a difference in concentration.

sections.heading: What affects the rate of diffusion

blocks.text: Four factors change how fast a substance diffuses.

rows: More particles move down the gradient than back up it
Particles have more energy and move faster
More particles can cross at the same time
Particles have less far to travel

diagram.alt: Move the sliders for surface area, concentration difference and membrane thickness to see how the relative rate of diffusion changes. The number is a comparison between settings, not a real measurement.

outputs.label: Relative rate of diffusion (a comparison, not a real measurement)

blocks.text: Keeping diffusion fast in the body

items: Gas exchange surfaces such as the alveoli are thin, one cell thick, so the diffusion distance is short.
A good blood supply keeps the concentration gradient steep by carrying substances away.
Ventilation brings fresh air in, which keeps the oxygen concentration high in the alveoli.
A steeper gradient, higher temperature and larger surface area all speed up diffusion.
A thicker membrane or longer distance slows diffusion down.
Exchange surfaces are thin and have a good blood supply.

blocks.text: Agar jelly cubes with a pink indicator turn clear when acid diffuses into them. The distance the clear area has spread shows how far the acid has diffused.

items.text: Use agar cubes of the same size, each containing the pink indicator.
Heat the hydrochloric acid to different temperatures.
Use the same volume and concentration of acid, and leave the cubes for the same time.
Measure the clear distance from the outside of each cube at each temperature.

blocks.label: Rate of diffusion
blocks.formula: rate of diffusion = distance diffused ÷ time

items.text: The acid diffused 3 mm in 120 s, so 3 ÷ 120.

items: Change one factor at a time, and control the others.
Measure the clear distance from the outside of the cube.
Rate = distance ÷ time.

checks.a: The spreading of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration (down a concentration gradient).

checks.q: Give two factors that affect the rate of diffusion.
checks.a: Any two from: concentration gradient, temperature, surface area, diffusion distance (thickness of the membrane).

worked_example.question: Diffusion is an important process in animals and plants. What is meant by the term diffusion?
answer_points: The movement or spreading of molecules or particles.
From a higher concentration to a lower concentration (down the concentration gradient).
worked_example.tip: Do not write movement "from a concentration gradient". References to membranes are ignored.

worked_example.question: Devise a method, using cubes of agar jelly, to investigate how temperature affects the rate of diffusion.
answer_points: Heat (hydrochloric) acid to different temperatures (or heat the agar jelly cubes).
Use agar jelly cubes of the same size.
Use the same volume and concentration of acid.
Leave them for the same amount of time.
Measure the clear distance from the outside of the cube at each temperature.
worked_example.tip: Any three score one mark each. "Amount of acid" is ignored.

blocks.text: You must be able to state how the three factors combine. The slider above uses this relationship.

blocks.label: Fick's law
blocks.formula: rate of diffusion ∝ (surface area × concentration difference) ÷ thickness of the membrane
where: Doubling the surface area or the concentration difference doubles the rate.
Doubling the thickness halves the rate.

worked_example.question: The substances transported around the organism enter cells either by active transport, diffusion or osmosis. For each substance indicate which method of transport is used. Substances: water moving into guard cells; mineral ions moving into root hair cells against a concentration gradient; oxygen entering red blood cells.
answer_points: Water moving into guard cells: osmosis.
Mineral ions moving into root hair cells against a concentration gradient: active transport.
Oxygen entering red blood cells: diffusion.
worked_example.tip: One mark for each correct row. Only water moves by osmosis, and "against a concentration gradient" means active transport.

rows: Down a concentration gradient, no energy needed
Against a concentration gradient, uses energy

worked_example.question:
Cubes of agar jelly can be used as model cells.
Agar jelly cubes are colourless and can be stained pink with an indicator. When placed in an acid solution, the acid diffuses into the agar jelly cubes and the pink colour starts to disappear. When the acid has reached the centre of the agar jelly cube, the agar is completely colourless.
Plan an investigation to determine the effect of temperature on the rate of diffusion in model cells.
answer_points: Independent variable: use at least two different temperatures.
Method: a way of keeping the acid at each temperature, such as a water bath.
Cut the agar into cubes of the same size, and use enough acid to cover the cubes.
Keep constant: size and shape of the cubes, type of agar, concentration (pH) and volume of acid, type of indicator (maximum three).
Dependent variable: the time taken for the cube to become completely colourless.
Repeat at least twice more.
Give a safety precaution, such as wearing goggles or cutting the agar away from the hands.
worked_example.tip: Marks are for the variable you change, the variables you control, what you measure, repeats and safety.

items: The energy for diffusion comes from the **kinetic energy** of the random movement of molecules and ions.
Because the particles move at random, more of them move down the concentration gradient than up it.

(Supplement) In the placenta, dissolved nutrients and oxygen diffuse from the mother's blood into the fetus's blood. Carbon dioxide and urea diffuse the other way. The umbilical cord carries the fetus's blood to and from the placenta.

worked_example.question:
A cell is shaped like a cube. Each side has a length of 0.053 mm.
Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of this cell.
Give your answer in the form n : 1
answer_points: Surface area to volume ratio = 0.016 854 ÷ 0.000 148 877 = 113 : 1 (to 3 significant figures).
worked_example.tip: Marks are for the volume, the surface area and the ratio.

blocks.text: The size of a cell changes how fast substances can enter it, because of its surface area to volume ratio.

items: For a cube, surface area = 6 × side², and volume = side³.
A larger ratio means more surface for each unit of volume, so diffusion in and out is faster for the whole cell.
Small cells and flattened or folded shapes have a larger ratio than big cells.

items.text: Surface area = 6 cm² and volume = 1 cm³, so the ratio is 6 : 1. The smaller cube has the larger ratio.
